The Two-Color Ext Soergel Calculus
or: The Ext-Dihedral Cathedral

Abstract
We compute Ext groups between Soergel Bimodules associated to the infinite/finite dihedral group for a realization in characteristic 0 and show that they are free right R − R- modules. In particular, we obtain an explicit diagrammatic basis for the Hochschild cohomology of indecomposable Soergel Bimodules. We then give a diagrammatic presentation for the corresponding monoidal category of Ext-enhanced Soergel Bimodules. As applications, we explicitly compute HOMFLY homology/triply graded link homology HHH ¯ \overline{\mathrm{HHH}} for the connect sum of two Hopf links and the negative torus link T ⁡ ( 3 , − 3 ) T(3,-3) as right R − R- modules. Furthermore, we show that the Hochschild cohomology of Soergel Bimodules in finite dihedral type categorifies Gomi’s trace, providing a t − t- analog of Soergel’s Hom Formula in the dihedral setting.



1
Introduction

The story of Soergel Bimodules had it’s birthplace in the work of Wolfgang Soergel in the 1990s
[
Soe90
]
as an alternative algebraic approach to proving the illustrious Kazhdan-Lusztig (KL) conjectures
[
KL79
]
and to give a combinatorial description of Harish-Chandra bimodules
[
Soe92
]
. Soergel Bimodules have a relatively straightforward definition, yet they have had profound applications in representation theory, geometry and link homology, especially in recent years. Conceptually, this arises from the fact that Soergel Bimodules categorify the Hecke Algebra, and the Hecke Algebra is a fundamental object of study within these fields.

1.1
History

Let
(W,S)
be a Coxeter group and
\mathbf{H}_{W}
be its associated Hecke Algebra. When
W
is the Weyl group for a split torus
T
of a reductive group
G
, It has two well-known bases over
\mathbb{Z}[v^{\pm 1}]
, the
standard basis

\left\{\delta_{w}\right\}_{w\in W}
and the
Kazhdan-Lusztig basis

\left\{b_{w}\right\}_{w\in W}
. In
[
KL79
]
, Kazhdan and Lusztig made their astonishing conjecture that the change of basis matrix between
\left\{b_{w}\right\}_{w\in W}
and
\left\{\delta_{x}\right\}_{x\in W}
at
v=1
equals the matrix of Jordan-Hölder multiplicities of simples in Verma modules in
\mathcal{O}_{0}(\mathfrak{g})
, the principal block of Category
\mathcal{O}
for
\mathfrak{g}
, the lie algebra of
G
. This conjecture was then proved by Beilinson–Bernstein
[
BB81
]
, and Brylinski–Kashiwara
[
BK81
]
by employing deep geometric techniques, such as the usage of the Decomposition Theorem.

A key role in the proofs is played by
\mathcal{H}_{W}
, the (geometric) Hecke category, a certain monoidal subcategory of
D^{b}_{B\times B}(G,\mathbb{C})
, the
B\times B
equivariant derived category of sheaves on
G
with
\mathbb{C}
coefficients. As the name suggests,
\mathcal{H}_{W}
is a categorification of the Hecke algebra. By categorification, we mean that there is an isomorphism of algebras

\displaystyle K_{\oplus}(\mathcal{H}_{W})\cong\mathbf{H}_{W}

(1)

where
K_{\oplus}(\mathcal{H}_{W})
is the split Grothendieck group of
\mathcal{H}_{W}
. In the early 1990s, Soergel
[
Soe92
]
gave another incarnation of the Hecke category
\mathcal{H}_{W}
that was more ”algebraic.” Specifically, let
\mathfrak{t}=\mathrm{Lie}(T)
and
R=\mathrm{Sym}(\mathfrak{t}^{*})
. Because
H^{\bullet}_{B\times B}(\mathrm{pt})\cong R\otimes_{\mathbb{C}}R
, equivariant hypercohomology of any object in
D^{b}_{B\times B}(G,\mathbb{C})
is naturally a graded module over
R\otimes_{\mathbb{C}}R
. Since
R
is commutative, hypercohomology is therefore a functor
\mathbb{H}^{\bullet}_{B\times B}:\mathcal{H}_{W}\to R-\mathrm{Bim}
. Soergel’s key observation is that
\mathbb{H}^{\bullet}_{B\times B}
is fully-faithful and monoidal and as a result we have a monoidal equivalence

\mathcal{H}_{W}\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Bim}(\mathfrak{t},W)

where
\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Bim}
is the category of
Soergel bimodules
, a monoidal subcategory of
R-\mathrm{Bim}
given by the essential image of
\mathbb{H}^{\bullet}_{B\times B}
. Using this equivalence (or rather a similar equivalence with Soergel modules), Soergel
[
Soe90
]
shows how the KL conjectures would follow from a certain desired property of
\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Bim}(\mathfrak{t},W)
called
Soergel’s Conjecture
.

In fact, Soergel gives a completely algebraic definition of
\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Bim}
in his work above. Specifically,
W
acts on
\mathfrak{t}
and thus on
R
via graded algebra automorphisms. Let
R^{s}\subset R
be the subalgebra of elements of
R
invariant under
s\in S
. Define the
R-
bimodule
B_{s}=R\otimes_{R^{s}}R(1)
.
\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Bim}
is then equivalent to the smallest full additive monoidal Karoubian graded subcategory of
R-\mathrm{Bim}
containing
B_{s}
for each
s\in S
. Thus, the definition above allows us to define
\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Bim}(\mathfrak{h},W)
for
any
Coxeter group
W
and
any
representation
\mathfrak{h}
. Moreover in
[
Soe07
]
, Soergel shows that when
\mathfrak{h}
is “reflection faithful”,
\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Bim}(\mathfrak{h},W)
categorifies
\mathbf{H}_{W}
. In other words, there is an isomorphism of algebras

\mathbf{H}_{W}\cong K_{\oplus}(\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Bim}(\mathfrak{h},W))

In this setting, the statement of Soergel’s conjecture still makes sense and Soergel shows that this would imply a major open question in combinatorics: the Kazhdan-Lusztig positivity conjecture for arbitrary Coxeter groups.

However, lacking the Decomposition Theorem in this setting, he was unable to prove his conjecture.

Fortunately
\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Bim}(\mathfrak{t},W)
is a monoidal category, and thus one can hope to give a presentation by generators modulo local relations. Using the language of planar diagrammatics, this was first done by Elias-Khovanov in
[
EK10
]
for
W=S_{n}
, by Elias
[
Eli16
]
in the dihedral case and finally by Elias-Williamson
[
EW16
]
for any Coxeter group
W
. Although the presentation was found using Soergel bimodules, the resulting monoidal category can be considered independently, thus giving a third incarnation of the Hecke category
\mathscr{D}(\mathfrak{h},W)
, referred to as the diagrammatic Hecke category. This incarnation has the advantage that many complicated computations can be reduced to algorithmic manipulations of planar diagrams. Using the diagrammatic Hecke category, Elias and Williamson
[
EW14
]
were able to prove Soergel’s conjecture for any Coxeter group
W
thereby proving the Kazhdan-Lusztig positivity conjecture and completing Soergel’s purely algebraic proof of the Kazhdan-Lusztig conjectures. The diagrammatic Hecke category has subsequently led to other breakthroughs in representation theory such as Williamson’s counterexamples
[
Wil17
]
to the long-standing Lusztig’s conjecture (the analogue of the KL conjectures for representations of reductive algebraic groups in characteristic
p
) and the subsequent new character formulas for irreducible and indecomposable tilting modules conjectured in
[
RW18
]
and proved in
[
RW18
]
and
[
AMRW19
]
.

In type
A
, the Hecke algebra
\mathbf{H}_{S_{n}}
also plays an important role in knot theory in the construction of link invariants. Given a link
L
written as the closure of a braid
\beta_{L}\in\mathrm{Br}_{n}
, Jones
[
Jon87
]
shows that the HOMFLY polynomial of
L
is “essentially equal” to
\mathrm{Tr}(\pi(\beta_{L}))
where
\pi:B_{n}\to\mathbf{H}_{S_{n}}
and
\mathrm{Tr}
is the Jones-Ocneanu trace on
\mathbf{H}_{S_{n}}
. Khovanov
[
Kho07
]
would later categorify this construction to produce a triply graded link homology theory as follows. For a braid
\beta_{L}\in B_{n}
, there is an associated (Rouquier) complex
F(\beta_{L})\in K^{b}(\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Bim}(\mathbb{C}^{n},S_{n}))
(categorification of
\mathbf{H}_{S_{n}}
) where
\mathbb{C}^{n}
is the permutation representation of
S_{n}
. Khovanov then applies the functor of Hochschild cohomology (categorification of
\mathrm{Tr}
) to
F(\beta_{L})
and takes cohomology to produce the desired link homology
\mathrm{HHH}(\beta_{L})
. In recent years there has been a great deal of interest surrounding
\mathrm{HHH}(\beta_{L})
as it turns out to have deep connections with Hilbert Schemes
[
ORS18
]
,
[
GNR21
]
,
[
GH22
]
rational Cherednik algebras
[
GORS14
]
and rational Catalan combinatorics
[
Hog17
]
,
[
HM19
]
,
[
GMV20
]
.
Needless to say, Soergel Bimodules and the diagrammatic Hecke category are at the center of modern geometric representation theory and categorification.

1.2
Main Results

In this paper we give a diagrammatic presentation for the monoidal categories
\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Bim}^{\mathrm{Ext}}(\mathfrak{h},W_{\infty}),\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Bim}^{\mathrm{Ext}}(\mathfrak{h},W_{m})
of Ext-enhanced Soergel Bimodules for the infinite and finite dihedral group
W_{\infty}
and
W_{m}
(we will abbreviate both cases using the notation
W_{\infty/m}
) for a realization
\mathfrak{h}
in characteristic 0 satisfying the usual 2-color assumptions + a linear independence condition. This paper builds upon the
A_{1}
case done by Shotaro Makisumi in
[
Mak22
]
. We will give some clarifications on the monoidal structure later, but for now note that extending/replacing the graded Hom spaces in
\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Bim}(\mathfrak{h},W_{\infty/m})
via

\mathrm{Hom}_{R-\mathrm{Bim}}^{\bullet}(-,-)\leadsto\mathrm{Ext}_{R-\mathrm{Bim}}^{\bullet,\bullet}(-,-)

still results in a category
\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Bim}^{\mathrm{Ext}}(\mathfrak{h},W_{\infty/m})
with composition given by the Yoneda product. This still has a monoidal structure (or rather super-monoidal structure as explained in
[
Mak22
]
) and in addition to the Elias-Khovanov generators we have (essentially) three additional one-color generators pictured below using planar diagrammatics

\mathscr{D}^{\mathrm{Ext}}(\mathfrak{h},W_{\infty/m})
. To be more precise, as in
[
EK10
]
and

EW16

\textnormal{BSBim}^{\mathrm{Ext}}(\mathfrak{h},W_{\infty/m})
, the full subcategory of
D^{b}(R-\mathrm{Bim})
1
1

1

Minor technicality, Hom spaces in
\textnormal{BSBim}^{\mathrm{Ext}}(\mathfrak{h},W_{\infty/m})
will actually be
\bigoplus_{n}\mathrm{Hom}_{D^{b}(R-\mathrm{Bim})}(M,N[n])
.
with objects the Bott-Samelson bimodules from which
\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Bim}^{\mathrm{Ext}}(\mathfrak{h},W_{\infty/m})
can be recovered by taking the Karoubian envelope. One main result of the paper will then be the following equivalences

\mathscr{D}^{\mathrm{Ext}}(\mathfrak{h},W_{\infty})\simeq\textnormal{BSBim}^{\mathrm{Ext}}(\mathfrak{h},W_{\infty}),\qquad\mathscr{D}^{\mathrm{Ext}}(\mathfrak{h},W_{m})\simeq\textnormal{BSBim}^{\mathrm{Ext}}(\mathfrak{h},W_{m})

Note that although the categories
\mathscr{D}^{\mathrm{Ext}}(\mathfrak{h},W_{\infty/m})
can be considered when
\mathfrak{h}
has characteristic
p
, it is not clear to the author that the same equivalences above still hold, as there appears to be more generators in
\textnormal{BSBim}^{\mathrm{Ext}}(\mathfrak{h},W_{\infty/m})
. In the course of the proof we obtain a complete description of Hom spaces in
\textnormal{BSBim}^{\mathrm{Ext}}(\mathfrak{h},W_{\infty/m})
. Specifically for any two expressions
\underline{v},\underline{w}
, we will compute

\mathrm{Ext}_{R-\mathrm{Bim}}^{\bullet,\bullet}(\mathrm{BS}(\underline{v}),\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))

as a right
R
module (although the results can be equivalently stated with the left
R-
module structure) (see
Theorem

3.13
,
Theorem

7.2
). In particular the morphism space above will always be free as a right
R-
module. When
m=2,3,4,6
this is also a special case of
[
WW11
]
which uses geometric methods that do not apply when
W_{m}
is non-crystallographic. In fact, we are able to obtain an explicit basis for
\mathrm{Ext}^{\bullet,\bullet}_{R-\mathrm{Bim}}(R,B_{w})
where
B_{w}
is an indecomposable Soergel Bimodule (see
Theorem

5.6
).

One thing to note is that throughout the algebraic portion of the paper, diagrammatics are already present, first as a visual aid to help explain the new relations, and then used in proofs of theorems which live in the algebraic category. This is allowed, however, as each time we are either using the equivalence
\mathscr{D}(\mathfrak{h},W_{\infty/m})\simeq\textnormal{BSBim}(\mathfrak{h},W_{\infty/m})
established in
[
Eli16
]
or a previously established relation in
\textnormal{BSBim}^{\mathrm{Ext}}(\mathfrak{h},W_{\infty/m})
of which we had a diagrammatic interpretation of. When the expression for a relation in
\textnormal{BSBim}^{\mathrm{Ext}}(\mathfrak{h},W_{\infty/m})
is not too cumbersome, we will write it out explicitly, and accompany it with a diagrammatic description.

1.2.1
Applications

(a)

Because Hochschild cohomology of a
R-
bimodule
M
is defined to be
\mathrm{HH}^{k}(M):=\mathrm{Ext}_{R-\mathrm{Bim}}^{k}(R,M)
one can apply our results to compute triply graded link homology
\mathrm{HHH}(\beta_{L})
where
\beta_{L}
is a braid on 3 strands by setting
\mathfrak{h}=\mathbb{C}^{3}(\mathbb{C}^{2})
to be the permutation (geometric) realization of
S_{3}
. This yields a new technique for computing
\mathrm{HHH}
, and can be visualized schematically as follows:
\mathrm{HHH}^{A=k}
is cohomology of the following chain complex

\ldots\to\mathrm{HH}^{k}(F(\beta)_{i})\xrightarrow{d_{i}}\mathrm{HH}^{k}(F(\beta)_{i+1})\to\ldots\vskip-12.91663pt\vskip 4.30554pt\qquad\qquad\text{(homological algebra)}

\leadsto

Theorem

5.6

\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\ \ldots\to R^{\ell_{i}}\xrightarrow{\lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{finequiv}}R^{\ell_{i+1}}\to\ldots\vskip-12.91663pt\vskip 4.30554pt\qquad\qquad\text{(linear algebra over }R)\vskip 4.30554pt

An upshot of this technique is that it doesn’t require
\mathrm{HHH}
to be parity
2
2

2

Concentrated in only even or only odd
T-
degrees.
which is crucial for the method in
[
EH19
]
used to compute
\mathrm{HHH}
of positive torus links. Thus our technique allows for new computations of
\mathrm{HHH}
not in the literature. For example in
Appendix

B
, we compute
\mathrm{HHH}
of the negative torus link
T(3,-3)
.

In
[
Li25
]
we go beyond 3 strands by computing
\mathrm{HHH}
of any positive or negative braid on
n
strands in certain
T-
degrees. Also, unlike in
[
EH19
]
which can only compute
\mathrm{HHH}
as a vector space, our method computes
\mathrm{HHH}
as
R-
modules. This capability is vital in our computation of
\mathrm{HHH}(T(3,-3))
. See
[
HM19
, Problem 1.12, Section 1.1.2]
for more on the importance of computing
\mathrm{HHH}
as an
R-
module.

(b)

In
[
Gom06
]
, Gomi generalizes the two variable Jones-Ocneanu trace on
\mathbf{H}_{S_{n}}
to a trace on
\mathbf{H}_{W}
satisfying a “Markov” type condition, where
W
is any finite Coxeter group as follows. Because
\mathbf{H}_{W}
is semisimple any trace
\tau:\mathbf{H}_{W}\to\mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}][t]
can be written as

\tau=\sum_{\chi\in\mathrm{Irr}W}w^{\chi}\chi_{q}

Gomi then defines
w^{\chi}:\mathbf{H}_{W}\to\mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}][t]
using entries from Lusztig’s Fourier transform matrix
S
. When
W
is the Weyl group of a reductive algebraic group
G/\mathbb{F}_{q}
,
S
is the change of basis matrix between unipotent characters and almost characters for the finite group of Lie type
G^{F}

[
Lus84
]
. When
W
is of dihedral type,
S
is the Exotic Fourier transform of Lusztig
[
Lus94
]
. In
Appendix

C
we show that the Poincare series for the Hochschild cohomology of Soergel Bimodules for
W_{m}
coincides with Gomi’s trace defined above
3
3

3

We were informed by Minh-Tâm Trinh that a version of this was stated in the thesis of Lasy, with an incomplete proof.
which allows us to establish a
t-
analog of Soergel’s Hom Formula. For
m=2,3,4,6
this is a special case of
[
WW11
]
which uses properties of unipotent character sheaves. From this we speculate that a suitable category of Ext-enhanced Soergel Bimodules is the right setting for the study of ”spetses”
[
BMM99
]
.

(c)

Soergel Bimodules corresponding to
\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Bim}(\mathbb{C}^{n},S_{n})
have an alternative pictorial description that is 3D instead of 2D. Instead of depicting morphisms between Bott-Samelson bimodules using planar diagrams, we depict a Bott-Samelson bimodule
B_{i_{1}}\otimes_{R}\cdots\otimes_{R}B_{i_{d}}
as a planar diagram, see
[
Kho07
]
Figures 2,3. Morphisms can then be realized by linear combinations of foams
-
decorated two-dimensional CW-complexes embedded in
\mathbb{R}^{3}
that arise as cobordisms between the planar diagrams described above. Foams are one of the fundamental objects used in constructing link homology theories. They show up prominently in the doubly graded
\mathfrak{sl}_{n}
theories starting with
[
Kho04
]
in
\mathfrak{sl}_{3}
and
[
MSV09
]
,
[
QR16
]
for
\mathfrak{sl}_{n}
, and finally in
[
RW20
]
for equivariant
\mathfrak{sl}_{n}
.

One major step in the construction of all these link homology theories is to define some variant of foam evaluation for closed foams which is used to associate a vector space
F(\Gamma)
to a web. In
[
RW20a
]
, Robert and Wagner show that applying the variant,
F_{\infty}(\Gamma)
to a special class of foams recovers
\mathscr{B}(\Gamma)
the (singular) Soergel Bimodule corresponding to
\Gamma
. Moreover, they show that by closing the planar diagram first and then applying
F_{\infty}
recovers
\mathrm{HH}_{0}(\mathscr{B}(\Gamma))
. In
[
KRW
]
they extend this to
\mathrm{HH}_{k}(\mathscr{B}(\Gamma))
for all
k\geq 0
. As
\mathrm{HH}_{\bullet}(M)\cong\mathrm{HH}^{\bullet}(M)
for bimodules over polynomial rings, it would be interesting to see how our relations below can be realized in this framework.

(d)

A crucial step in the proof of the tilting character formula in
[
AMRW19
]

was to relate two different derived categories of sheaves. To do this the authors first establish an equivalence between two different monoidal categories which act on the different categories above. Specifically, using the diagrammatics developed in
[
EW16
]
, they establish monoidal Koszul duality with modular coefficients for any Kac-Moody group
\mathscr{G}
. For more details there is a nice introduction to these ideas in
[
Mak19
]
, but the key point right now is that there’s an equivalence of monoidal categories

\kappa^{mon}:(\mathscr{D}(\mathfrak{h},W),\star)\xrightarrow{\sim}(\mathrm{TiltFM}(\mathfrak{h}^{*},W),\widehat{\star})

giving rise to the doubly graded equivalence of categories

\kappa:K^{b}(\mathscr{D}(\mathfrak{h},W)\otimes_{R}\mathbbm{k})\xrightarrow{\sim}K^{b}(\mathbbm{k}\otimes_{R}\mathscr{D}(\mathfrak{h}^{*},W))

interchanging indecomposable and tilting objects such that
\kappa\circ(-1)[1]=(1)\circ\kappa
. In
[
HM20
]
Hogancamp and Makisumi conjecture that this can be extended to an equivalence of monoidal categories

(\kappa^{mon})^{\mathrm{Ext}}:(\mathscr{D}^{\mathrm{Ext}}(\mathfrak{h},W),\star)\overset{\sim}{\dashrightarrow}(\mathrm{TiltFM}^{\mathrm{Ext}}(\mathfrak{h}^{*},W),\widehat{\star})

giving rise to a triply graded equivalence of categories

\kappa^{\mathrm{Ext}}:K^{b}(\mathscr{D}^{\mathrm{Ext}}(\mathfrak{h},W)\otimes_{R}\mathbbm{k})\overset{\sim}{\dashrightarrow}K^{b}(\mathbbm{k}\otimes_{R}\mathscr{D}^{\mathrm{Ext}}(\mathfrak{h}^{*},W))

interchanging indecomposable and tilting objects such that
\kappa^{\mathrm{Ext}}\circ(-1)[1]=(1)\circ\kappa^{\mathrm{Ext}}
and provide evidence in the
\mathfrak{gl}_{2}
realization of
W=S_{2}
. The main results in this paper can therefore be used to help define
(\kappa^{mon})^{\mathrm{Ext}}
to prove such an equivalence. According to Makisumi, ”One may speculate that this triply-graded Koszul duality is connected to a duality for character sheaves.”

1.3
Organization

•

Background

\circ

In
Section

2
we review notation and conventions. In particular our notation for Koszul complexes will be important for our computations later on. Throughout the paper we will
always
assume the reader is familiar with Soergel bimodules and the two-color Soergel diagrammatics such as the light leaf morphisms. A good place to read up on this would be in
[
EMTW20
]
Chapters 4, 5, 9, 10, 12.

\circ

In
Section

2.3
we review the diagrammatics of the
A_{1}
case
\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Bim}^{\mathrm{Ext}}(\mathfrak{h},S_{2})
. For the computations done in this paper, it turns out that we only need that Theorem 5.2 in
[
Mak22
]
holds, i.e. the defining relations of
\mathscr{D}^{\mathrm{Ext}}(\mathfrak{h},S_{2})
hold in
\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Bim}^{\mathrm{Ext}}(\mathfrak{h},S_{2})
.

•

The Algebraic Category

\circ

In
Section

3
we compute
\mathrm{Ext}_{R^{e}}^{\bullet,\bullet}(B_{t},\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))
as a right
R-
module when
m_{st}=\infty
which will allow us to define the main new generating morphism
\Phi_{t}^{\underline{w}}
in
\textnormal{BSBim}^{\mathrm{Ext}}(\mathfrak{h},W_{\infty})
in
Section

4.2
. We should note that
\Phi_{t}^{\underline{w}}
doesn’t quite correspond to the new generator in the diagrammatic category (they are off by a rotation+possibly a sign) but it’s much easier to work with
\Phi_{t}^{\underline{w}}
in the algebraic category.

\circ

In
Section

5
we give an explicit basis for
\mathrm{Ext}_{R^{e}}^{\bullet,\bullet}(R,B_{w})
as a right
R
module which shows that
\mathrm{Ext}_{R^{e}}^{\bullet,\bullet}(R,B_{w})
is more or less controlled by
\mathrm{Hom}_{R^{e}}^{\bullet}(R,B_{w})
.

\circ

Section

7
proves a lot of the same theorems as above but now in the finite case
m_{st}<\infty
. In most cases, we just check that the argument for
m_{st}=\infty
still holds when
m_{st}<\infty
.

•

The Diagrammatic Category

\circ

In
Section

6
and
Section

8
we define the Ext-enhanced diagrammatic Hecke categories
\mathscr{D}^{\mathrm{Ext}}_{\infty}
and
\mathscr{D}^{\mathrm{Ext}}_{m_{st}}
associated to a (faithful) realization
\mathfrak{h}
of the infinite and finite dihedral groups
W_{\infty}
,
W_{m_{st}}
respectively. We will then establish the equivalences
\mathscr{D}^{\mathrm{Ext}}_{\infty}\simeq\textnormal{BSBim}^{\mathrm{Ext}}(\mathfrak{h},W_{\infty})
and
\mathscr{D}^{\mathrm{Ext}}_{m_{st}}\simeq\textnormal{BSBim}^{\mathrm{Ext}}(\mathfrak{h},W_{m_{st}})
. The proof bootstraps the proof of the dihedral equivalence in
[
Eli16
]
in that it just suffices to show the isomorphism

\mathrm{Hom}^{\bullet,\bullet}_{\mathscr{D}^{\mathrm{Ext}}_{\infty}}(\mathscr{B}_{\varnothing},\mathscr{B}_{w})\cong\mathrm{Ext}^{\bullet,\bullet}_{R^{e}}(R,B_{w})

and that we have a very explicit description of the rank 2 projectors to the indecomposable summands
B_{w}
given by the
Jones-Wenzl
projectors. Unlike in
[
Eli16
]
our proof relies on one of the main theorems in
[
EW16
]
, namely that double leaves form a right
R
basis for hom spaces in the diagrammatic Hecke category.

•

Appendices

\circ

In
Appendix

A
we define chain lifts for morphisms in
\mathbb{S}\textnormal{Bim}(\mathfrak{h},W)
. In
Appendix

B
we first compute HOMFLY homology for the connect sum of two Hopf links. Then we compute the HOMFLY homology for the negative torus link
T(3,-3)
. In
Appendix

C
we show that the Poincare series for Hochschild homology of Soergel Bimodules agrees with Gomi’s trace for
W=W_{m}
.

Preliminaries and Notation

2.1
Realizations and Gradings

We first recall the definition of a realization of a Coxeter system
(W,S)
as defined in
[
EW16
]
Section 3.

Definition 2.1
.

Let
\mathbbm{k}
be a commutative ring. A realization of
(W,S)
over
\mathbbm{k}
is a triple

\mathfrak{h}=(V,\left\{\alpha_{s}\right\}_{s\in S}\subset V^{*},\left\{\alpha_{s}^{\vee}\right\}_{s\in S}\subset V)

where
V
is a free, finite rank
\mathbbm{k}
module such that for
\left\langle-,-\right\rangle
the natural pairing between
V,V^{*}
,

(1)

\left\langle\alpha_{s}^{\vee},\alpha_{s}\right\rangle=2
for all
s\in S
.

(2)

The assignment
s(v)=v-\left\langle v,\alpha_{s}\right\rangle\alpha_{s}^{\vee}
for all
v\in V
yields a representation of
W
.

(3)

For each
s,t\in S
let
a_{st}:=\left\langle\alpha_{s}^{\vee},\alpha_{t}\right\rangle
and
m_{st}
the order of
st
in
W
. Then
[m_{st}]_{a_{st}}=[m_{st}]_{a_{ts}}=0
where
[k]_{x}
are the
2-
colored quantum numbers defined in Section 3 of
[
EW16
]
.

For the rest of the paper we will assume the following.

Assumption 1
.

\mathfrak{h}
is a balanced realization of rank
n
that satisfies Demazure surjectivity over an integral domain
\mathbbm{k}
.

All of our algebras and modules will be bigraded with the cohomological grading
[1]
and Soergel/internal grading
(1)
that shifts degree down 1, e.g.
M(1)_{d}=M_{d+1}
. If an element has degree
(a,b)
the first coordinate
a
will always be the cohomological degree while the second coordinate
b
will always be the internal degree. If an algebra/module has no grading shift such as
V
, it is in degree
(0,0)
. We will frequently use the combined shift
\llbracket 1\rrbracket:=[1](-2)
.

Definition 2.2
.

Let
R:=\mathrm{Sym}^{\bullet}(V^{*}(-2))
and let
R^{e}=R\otimes_{\mathbbm{k}}R
. Let
R^{ee}=R\otimes_{\mathbbm{k}}R\otimes_{\mathbbm{k}}R
and so on with
R^{eee}
, etc.

This paper deals with the case when
W=W_{m_{st}}
where
W_{m_{st}}
is the Coxeter group generated by simple reflections
s,t
with relation
(st)^{m_{st}}=1
.
W_{\infty}
will be the infinite dihedral group.

Definition 2.3
.

\otimes
will always mean
\otimes_{\mathbbm{k}}
while
\otimes_{s}
will mean
\otimes_{R^{s}}
.

Definition 2.4
.

Given two complexes
A^{\bullet}=\oplus_{p}A^{p},B^{\bullet}=\oplus_{p}B^{p}
of
R^{e}-
graded modules, define the bigraded Hom complex as

\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{R^{e}}(A^{\bullet},B^{\bullet})=\bigoplus_{i,j}\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}^{i,j}_{R^{e}}(A^{\bullet},B^{\bullet})=\bigoplus_{i,j}\prod_{p}\mathrm{Hom}_{R^{e}}(A^{p},B^{p+i}(j))

with differential
d^{n}:\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}^{n,j}_{R^{e}}(A^{\bullet},B^{\bullet})\to\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}^{n+1,j}_{R^{e}}(A^{\bullet},B^{\bullet})
given by

d^{n}(f)=d_{B^{\bullet}}\circ f+(-1)^{n+1}f\circ d_{A^{\bullet}}

2.2
Koszul Complexes

For
a\in R
, let
a^{e}:=a\otimes 1-1\otimes a\in R^{e}
. Given a sequence of homogeneous elements
a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\in R
where
|a_{i}|
is the internal degree of
a_{i}
, let
K(a_{1}^{e},\ldots,a_{n}^{e})=K(a_{1}^{e})\otimes_{R^{e}}\ldots\otimes_{R^{e}}K(a_{n}^{e})
be the following graded Koszul complex where
K(a_{i}^{e})
is the complex

K(a_{i}^{e})=[0\to R^{e}\underline{a_{i}}\xrightarrow{a_{i}^{e}}\boxed{R^{e}\underline{1}}\to 0]=[0\to R^{e}(-|a_{i}|)\xrightarrow{a_{i}^{e}}\boxed{R^{e}}\to 0]

where the boxed term is in cohomological degree 0 and we have underlined
a_{i}
and
1
as they are the “exterior” part. Specifically, the graded Koszul complex has the structure of a bigraded dga as
K(a_{i}^{e})=\Lambda^{\bullet}(\mathbbm{k}\underline{a_{i}}[1](-|a_{i}|))\boxtimes R^{e}
while
K(a_{1}^{e},\ldots,a_{n}^{e})=\Lambda^{\bullet}(\mathbbm{k}\underline{a_{1}}[1](-|a_{1}|)\oplus\ldots\mathbbm{k}\underline{a_{n}}[1](-|a_{n}|))\boxtimes R^{e}
where the differential is determined by
d(\underline{a_{i}})=\underline{1}\boxtimes a_{i}^{e}
and the graded Leibniz rule. Here we use the notation
\Lambda^{\bullet}(\underline{V})\boxtimes R^{e}:=\Lambda^{\bullet}(\underline{V})\otimes R^{e}
to distinguish the exterior algebra part from
R^{e}
. All elements of
\Lambda^{\bullet}(\underline{V})
will be underlined as well. The
R-
bimodule structure is given by only acting on the
R^{e}
part, i.e.
r\cdot(\underline{v}\boxtimes f\otimes g)\cdot r^{\prime}=\underline{v}\boxtimes rf\otimes gr^{\prime}
and when tensoring two Koszul complexes
\Lambda^{\bullet}(\underline{V_{1}})\boxtimes R^{e}
,
\Lambda^{\bullet}(\underline{V_{2}})\boxtimes R^{e}
over
R
(instead of
R^{e}
), we tensor the
\Lambda
and
R^{e}
parts separately, i.e

\Lambda^{\bullet}(\underline{V_{1}})\boxtimes R^{e}\otimes_{R}\Lambda^{\bullet}(\underline{V_{2}})\boxtimes R^{e}=\Lambda^{\bullet}(\underline{V_{1}})\otimes\Lambda^{\bullet}(\underline{V_{2}})\boxtimes R^{e}\otimes_{R}R^{e}=\Lambda^{\bullet}(\underline{V_{1}})\otimes\Lambda^{\bullet}(\underline{V_{2}})\boxtimes R^{ee}

Now the
R-
bimodule structure is given by acting on the leftmost and rightmost tensor factors of
R^{ee}
. We will use the shorthand
\underline{v^{(1)}}:=\underline{v}\otimes\underline{1}
for
v\in V_{1}
and likewise
\underline{w^{(2)}}:=\underline{1}\otimes\underline{w}
for
w\in V_{2}
.

Two Koszul complexes will be of great importance to us. As shown in
[
Mak22
]

q_{\varnothing}:K_{\varnothing}\to R
and
q_{s}:K_{s}\to B_{s}
will be projective resolutions of
R
and
B_{s}
as a
R-
bimodule where

\displaystyle K_{\varnothing}:=K(e_{1}^{e},\ldots,e_{n}^{e})

\displaystyle=\Lambda^{\bullet}(\underline{V^{*}}\llbracket 1\rrbracket)\boxtimes R^{e}

(2)

\displaystyle K_{s}:=K(\rho_{s}s(\rho_{s})^{e},e_{1}^{e},\ldots,e_{n-1}^{e})(1)

\displaystyle=\Lambda^{\bullet}(\mathbbm{k}\underline{\rho_{s}s(\rho_{s})}[1](-4)\oplus\underline{(V^{*})^{s}}\llbracket 1\rrbracket)\boxtimes R^{e}

(3)

where
\rho_{s}\in V^{*}
satisfies
\left\langle\alpha_{s}^{\vee},\rho_{s}\right\rangle=1
which exists by Demazure surjectivity and
\left\{e_{i}\right\}_{i=1}^{n-1}
is a basis for
(V^{*})^{s}
while
\left\{e_{i}\right\}_{i=1}^{n}
is a basis for
V^{*}
.
q_{\varnothing}
is the map sending
\underline{1}\boxtimes 1\otimes 1\mapsto 1\otimes_{R}1
and everything else to 0, and similarly with
q_{s}
.

Koszul complexes have natural chain maps given by contraction. Specifically, following
[
Mak22
]

Definition 2.5
.

Given
v\in V\llbracket-1\rrbracket
, define
v\mathbin{\acute{\frown}}(-):\Lambda^{\bullet}(V^{*}\llbracket 1\rrbracket)\to\Lambda^{\bullet}(V^{*}\llbracket 1\rrbracket)
by

v\mathbin{\acute{\frown}}(r_{1}\wedge\cdots\wedge r_{k})=\sum_{i=1}^{k}(-1)^{i+1}r_{i}(v)r_{1}\wedge\cdots\wedge\widehat{r_{i}}\wedge\cdots\wedge r_{k}

One can then check that
v_{1}\mathbin{\acute{\frown}}(-)
anticommutes with
v_{2}\mathbin{\acute{\frown}}(-)
and so there is an induced map
\xi\mathbin{\acute{\frown}}(-):\Lambda^{\bullet}(V^{*}\llbracket 1\rrbracket)\to\Lambda^{\bullet}(V^{*}\llbracket 1\rrbracket)
for any
\xi\in\Lambda^{\bullet}(V\llbracket-1\rrbracket)
. Similarly, one also obtains a map
w\mathbin{\acute{\frown}}(-):\Lambda^{\bullet}(V\llbracket-1\rrbracket)\to\Lambda^{\bullet}(V\llbracket-1\rrbracket)
for any
w\in\Lambda^{\bullet}(V^{*}\llbracket 1\rrbracket)
.

Therefore for any
\xi\in\Lambda^{\bullet}(V\llbracket-1\rrbracket)
, by extending
R^{e}
linearly, we obtain a map

\displaystyle\widetilde{\iota_{\xi}}:K_{\varnothing}

\displaystyle\to K_{\varnothing}

\displaystyle\underline{z}\boxtimes 1\otimes 1

\displaystyle\mapsto\xi\mathbin{\acute{\frown}}(\underline{z})\boxtimes 1\otimes 1

and because
\widetilde{\iota_{\xi}}
is a derivation on
K_{\varnothing}
it will automatically be a chain map. Let
\iota_{\xi}
be the induced map on cohomology. We also have similar contraction maps for the Koszul complex
K_{s}
and there is one in particular that will be of great importance, namely,

Definition 2.6
.

Define
\gamma_{s}^{\vee}:\mathbbm{k}\underline{\rho_{s}s(\rho_{s})}[1](-4)\oplus\underline{(V^{*})^{s}}\llbracket 1\rrbracket\to\mathbbm{k}
by
\gamma_{s}^{\vee}(\underline{\rho_{s}s(\rho_{s})})=1
and
\gamma_{s}^{\vee}(\underline{(V^{*})^{s}})=0
. Then define the chain map

\widetilde{\phi_{s}}=-\gamma_{s}^{\vee}\mathbin{\acute{\frown}}(-)\in\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{R^{e}}^{1,-4}(K_{s},K_{s})

and let
\phi_{s}
be the induced map on cohomology.

In
[
Mak22
]
it was shown that
\alpha_{s}^{\vee}\mathbin{\acute{\frown}}(-):\Lambda^{\bullet}(V^{*}\llbracket 1\rrbracket)\to\Lambda^{\bullet}(V^{*}\llbracket 1\rrbracket)
actually lands in
\Lambda^{\bullet}((V^{*})^{s}\llbracket 1\rrbracket)
. As a result, we can define

Definition 2.7
.

Define the chain map

\widetilde{\eta_{s}}^{\mathrm{Ext}}=\alpha_{s}^{\vee}\mathbin{\acute{\frown}}(-)\in\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{R^{e}}^{1,-3}(K_{\varnothing},K_{s})

and let
\eta_{s}^{\mathrm{Ext}}
be the induced map on cohomology.

Definition 2.8
.

Let
s\in S
. Define the exterior Demazure operator
\partial_{s}:\Lambda^{\bullet}(V\llbracket-1\rrbracket)\to\Lambda^{\bullet}(V\llbracket-1\rrbracket/\mathbbm{k}\alpha_{s}^{\vee})
as the composition

\Lambda^{\bullet}(V\llbracket-1\rrbracket)\xrightarrow{\alpha_{s}\mathbin{\acute{\frown}}(-)}\Lambda^{\bullet}(V\llbracket-1\rrbracket)\twoheadrightarrow\Lambda^{\bullet}(V\llbracket-1\rrbracket/\mathbbm{k}\alpha_{s}^{\vee})

2.3
Review of the
A_{1}
Case

In this section we review the main results from
[
Mak22
]
. We first recall the definition of the algebraic category
\textnormal{BSBim}^{\mathrm{Ext}}(\mathfrak{h},W)
.

Definition 2.9
.

Let
\mathbb{D}^{b}(R^{e}-\mathrm{gmod})
4
4

4

According to
Bernhard Keller, this is sometimes called the
\mathbb{Z}
-graded category associated with
D^{b}(R^{e}-\mathrm{gmod}).
be the category with underlying objects
D^{b}(R^{e}-\mathrm{gmod})
and morphism spaces

\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{D}^{b}(R^{e}-\mathrm{gmod})}(A^{\bullet},B^{\bullet})=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\mathrm{Hom}_{D^{b}(R^{e}-\mathrm{gmod})}(A^{\bullet},B^{\bullet}[n])

Definition 2.10
.

Given an expression
\underline{w}=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{m})
, define the corresponding Bott-Samelson complex to be

\mathrm{KS}(\underline{w})=\mathrm{KS}(s_{1},\ldots,s_{m}):=K_{s_{1}}\otimes_{R}\ldots\otimes_{R}K_{s_{m}}

Then
\textnormal{BSBim}^{\mathrm{Ext}}(\mathfrak{h},W)
is the smallest full, additive, graded subcategory of
\mathbb{D}^{b}(R^{e}-\mathrm{gmod})
consisting of complexes isomorphic to Bott-Samelson complexes.

Lemma 2.11
.

q_{\underline{w}}:\mathrm{KS}(s_{1},\ldots,s_{m})\xrightarrow{q_{s_{1}}\otimes_{R}\ldots\otimes_{R}q_{s_{m}}}\mathrm{BS}(s_{1},\ldots,s_{m})
is a free
R^{e}
resolution.

Proof.

Proceed by induction on
m
. Note that any free
R^{e}
resolution will also be a free left or right
R-
module resolution. So by induction we see that

H^{k}(\mathrm{KS}(s_{1},\ldots,s_{m-1})\otimes_{R}K_{s_{m}})=\mathrm{Tor}^{R}_{k}(\mathrm{BS}(s_{1},\ldots,s_{m-1})_{R},{}_{R}B_{s_{m}})

where
\mathrm{BS}(s_{1},\ldots,s_{m-1})_{R}
is the left
R
module given by the right action of
R
, aka
r\star m=m\cdot r
for
m\in\mathrm{BS}(s_{1},\ldots,s_{m-1})_{R}
. But since all Bott-Samelson bimodules are free left or right
R
modules, we see that for
k>0
the RHS is 0 and for
k=0
, we have

H^{0}(\mathrm{KS}(s_{1},\ldots,s_{m-1})\otimes_{R}K_{s_{m}})=\mathrm{BS}(s_{1},\ldots,s_{m-1})\otimes_{R}B_{s_{m}}

as sets. But since the morphisms involved were
R^{e}-
linear it follows that the above is a bimodule isomorphism and so
\mathrm{KS}(s_{1},\ldots,s_{m})
is a free
R^{e}
resolution of
\mathrm{BS}(s_{1},\ldots,s_{m})
as desired
∎

Thus as
\mathrm{KS}(s_{1},\ldots,s_{m})
is a complex of projective
R^{e}
modules that resolves the bimodule
\mathrm{BS}(s_{1},\ldots,s_{m})
it follows that

\mathrm{Hom}_{\textnormal{BSBim}^{\mathrm{Ext}}(\mathfrak{h},W)}(\mathrm{KS}(s_{1},\ldots,s_{m}),\mathrm{KS}(r_{1},\ldots,r_{k}))\cong\mathrm{Ext}^{\bullet,\bullet}_{R^{e}}(\mathrm{BS}(s_{1},\ldots,s_{m}),\mathrm{BS}(r_{1},\ldots,r_{k}))

As mentioned in the introduction, we could have equivalently defined
\textnormal{BSBim}^{\mathrm{Ext}}(\mathfrak{h},W)
as replacing
\mathrm{Hom}
spaces with
\mathrm{Ext}
groups. However, the (super)-monoidal structure will then be
\otimes^{L}_{R}
of complexes. The upshot of the definition above
5
5

5

aka choosing a fixed projective resolution for each object.
is that the (super)monoidal structure is just simply the
\otimes_{R}
of complexes and composition is just composition of chain complexes instead of the Yoneda product.

As each
\mathrm{KS}(s_{1},\ldots,s_{m})
is a complex of projective
R^{e}-
modules any morphism in the Soergel category
\textnormal{BSBim}(\mathfrak{h},W)
will automatically lift to a morphism (unique up to homotopy) in
\textnormal{BSBim}^{\mathrm{Ext}}(\mathfrak{h},W)
and
\textnormal{BSBim}(\mathfrak{h},W)
embeds inside
\textnormal{BSBim}^{\mathrm{Ext}}(\mathfrak{h},W)
fully faithfully as the cohomological degree 0 part.

Thus we can and will use the RHS above for our computations involving
in the algebraic category instead of
\phi_{s}\circ\left[\widetilde{\eta_{s}}\right]
. It is important to note that
\textnormal{BSBim}(\mathfrak{h},S_{2})
only sits inside of
\textnormal{BSBim}^{\mathrm{Ext}}(\mathfrak{h},S_{2})
isomorphically, with objects
B_{s}
replaced by the dga
K_{s}
and morphisms replaced by their cohomology class of their chain lifts. Likewise, throughout the rest of the paper diagrammatics traditionally representing morphisms in
\textnormal{BSBim}(\mathfrak{h},W)
will instead refer to their corresponding morphism in
\textnormal{BSBim}^{\mathrm{Ext}}(\mathfrak{h},W)
.

2.4
Action of Exterior Boxes

Here we explain what diagrams with exterior boxes mean in
\textnormal{BSBim}^{\mathrm{Ext}}(\mathfrak{h},W)
. Given
\xi\in\Lambda^{\bullet}(V\llbracket-1\rrbracket)
we have that

K_{s}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces K_{\varnothing}\otimes_{R}K_{s}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces K_{\varnothing}\otimes_{R}K_{s}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces K_{s}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{\lambda_{s}}\ }
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{\iota_{\xi}}\otimes_{R}\mathrm{id}\ }

\scriptstyle\displaystyle\xi

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ \ =}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{\tau_{s}}\ }

\widetilde{\tau_{s}}
is the chain lift for the inverse of the left unitor as defined in
Appendix

A
and
\widetilde{\lambda_{s}}

B_{s}

\widetilde{\lambda_{s}}=K_{\varnothing}\otimes_{R}K_{s}\xrightarrow{q_{\varnothing}\otimes_{R}\mathrm{id}}R\otimes_{R}K_{s}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{mult}}K_{s}

3
Computation of
\mathrm{Ext}^{\bullet,\bullet}_{R^{e}}(B_{t},\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))
for
m_{st}=\infty

3.1
Warm-Up computation of
\mathrm{Ext}^{\bullet,\bullet}_{R^{e}}(R,B_{s})

Lemma 3.1
.

Let
B
be a
R^{e}-
module and suppose there is a subset
J\subset[n]
s.t.
a_{j}^{e}=0\text{ in }B\ \forall j\in J
, then there is an isomorphism of complexes as bigraded right
R-
modules .

\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{R^{e}}(K(a_{1}^{e},\ldots,a_{n}^{e}),B)\cong\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{R^{e}}(\otimes_{i\not\in J}K(a_{i}^{e}),B)\otimes_{\mathbbm{k}}\Lambda^{\bullet}\left(\oplus_{j\in J}\mathbbm{k}\underline{a_{j}}[1](-|a_{j}|)\right)^{*}

where the right
R-
module structure is given by
(f\cdot r)(x)=f(x)\cdot r
.

Proof.

We have the following chain of isomorphism of complexes

\displaystyle\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{R^{e}}(\otimes_{i\not\in J}K(a_{i}^{e})\otimes_{R^{e}}\otimes_{j\in J}K(a_{j}^{e}),B)

\displaystyle\cong\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{R^{e}}(\otimes_{i\not\in J}K(a_{i}^{e}),\ \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{R^{e}}(\otimes_{j\in J}K(a_{j}^{e}),B))

\displaystyle\cong\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{R^{e}}(\otimes_{i\not\in J}K(a_{i}^{e}),\Lambda^{\bullet}(\oplus_{j\in J}\mathbbm{k}\underline{a_{j}}[1](-|a_{j}|))^{*}\otimes_{\mathbbm{k}}B)

\displaystyle\cong\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{R^{e}}(\otimes_{i\not\in J}K(a_{i}^{e}),B)\otimes_{\mathbbm{k}}\Lambda^{\bullet}(\oplus_{j\in J}\mathbbm{k}\underline{a_{j}}[1](-|a_{j}|))^{*}

where the isomorphisms arise from the differential of the complex
\Lambda^{\bullet}(\oplus_{j\in J}\mathbbm{k}\underline{a_{j}}[1](-|a_{j}|))^{*}\otimes_{\mathbbm{k}}B
being 0 since
a_{j}^{e}=0
in
B
. It is easy to check that these are all maps of right
R-
modules.
∎

3.2
Main Computation

Let red correspond to the simple reflection
s
and blue correspond to the simple reflection
t
. Let
\underline{w}
be an arbitrary expression in
s
and
t
. For the rest of the paper we will also assume

Assumption 2
.

\exists\rho_{s},\rho_{t}\in V^{*}
such that
\left\langle\alpha_{s}^{\vee},\rho_{s}\right\rangle=1=\left\langle\alpha_{t}^{\vee},\rho_{t}\right\rangle
and
\left\langle\alpha_{s}^{\vee},\rho_{t}\right\rangle=0=\left\langle\alpha_{t}^{\vee},\rho_{s}\right\rangle
.

In particular, this means that
\rho_{s}\in(V^{*})^{t}
and that
\rho_{t}\in(V^{*})^{s}
.

Remark
.

This assumption is satisfied for both
\mathbb{C}^{n}
, the permutation realization, and the geometric realization for
W_{m_{st}}
. This assumption is also satisfied for the Kac-Moody realization for
W_{\infty}
, as the coroots
\left\{\alpha_{s}^{\vee}\right\}
of the realization are linearly independent.

Lemma 3.4
.

Let
F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathrm{End}(\mathcal{C})
be a monoidal functor from
(\mathcal{A},\otimes)
a monoidal category to the category of endofunctors of a category
\mathcal{C}
. Suppose we have objects
a_{1},a_{2}\in\mathcal{A}
such that
a_{1}\otimes(-)
is left adjoint to
a_{2}\otimes(-)
in
\mathcal{A}
, then

\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(F_{a_{1}}(c),c^{\prime})\cong\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(c,F_{a_{2}}(c^{\prime}))

Proof.

We need to give a unit and counit map satisfying the triangle identities. Since
F
is monoidal, we see that
F_{a_{2}}\circ F_{a_{1}}=F_{a_{2}\otimes a_{1}}
and thus the unit map will just come from applying
F
to the unit map in
\mathcal{A}
,
\mathds{1}\to a_{2}\otimes a_{1}
and similarly with the counit map and because
F
is a functor these will satisfy the triangle identities.
∎

Corollary 3.5
.

Let
M,N\in\textnormal{BSBim}(\mathfrak{h},W)
. Then we have a natural isomorphism of right
R-
modules,

\mathrm{Ext}^{\bullet,\bullet}_{R^{e}}(B_{t}\otimes_{R}M,N)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathrm{Ext}^{\bullet,\bullet}_{R^{e}}(M,B_{t}\otimes_{R}N)

Proof.

Apply the above lemma where
\mathcal{A}=\textnormal{BSBim}(\mathfrak{h},W)
,
\mathcal{C}=\textnormal{BSBim}^{\mathrm{Ext}}(\mathfrak{h},W)
and
F
is defined on objects as
F(B_{s})=K_{s}\otimes_{R}(-)
and then extended monoidally. On morphisms
F(f)=\widetilde{f}
, where
\widetilde{f}
is any chain lift of
f
. Now use that
B_{t}\otimes(-)
is biadjoint to itself with unit
u_{t}
. Then the isomorphism above is given by is given by
f\mapsto f\circ(u_{t}\otimes_{R}\mathrm{id}_{M})
which is clearly right
R-
linear.
∎

Our goal is to compute
\mathrm{Ext}^{\bullet,\bullet}_{R^{e}}(\mathrm{BS}(\underline{v}),\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))
but as seen above it suffices to compute Hochschild cohomology
\mathrm{Ext}^{\bullet,\bullet}_{R^{e}}(R,\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))
. However it also suffices to compute
\mathrm{Ext}^{\bullet,\bullet}_{R^{e}}(B_{t},\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))
for all
\underline{w}
and this turns out to be easier. Because of
2
,
\rho_{s},\rho_{t}
will be linearly independent, so we can decompose
V^{*}=\mathbbm{k}\rho_{s}\oplus\mathbbm{k}\rho_{t}\oplus(V^{*})^{s,t}
as
s,t
are reflections and thus fix a subspace of codimension 1. Let
\Lambda_{st}=\Lambda^{\bullet}((V^{*})^{s,t}\llbracket 1\rrbracket)^{*}\cong\Lambda^{\bullet}(V\llbracket-1\rrbracket/(\mathbbm{k}\alpha_{s}^{\vee}\oplus\mathbbm{k}\alpha_{t}^{\vee}))
. As such the resolution of
B_{t}
given in
Eq.

3
can be written as

K_{t}=K(\rho_{t}t(\rho_{t})^{e},\rho_{s}^{e},e_{1}^{e},\ldots,e_{n-2}^{e})(1)

where
\left\{e_{i}\right\}_{i=1}^{n-2}
is a basis for
(V^{*})^{s,t}
. As
e_{i}^{e}=0
on
\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w})
when
e_{i}\in(V^{*})^{s,t}
we can use
Lemma

3.1
to obtain

Theorem 3.6
.

We have an isomorphism of bigraded right
R
modules,

\mathrm{Ext}^{\bullet,\bullet}_{R^{e}}(B_{t},\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))\cong H^{\bullet}(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{R^{e}}(K(\rho_{t}t(\rho_{t})^{e},\rho_{s}^{e})(1),\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w})))\otimes_{\mathbbm{k}}\Lambda_{st}

As in the previous section, this decomposition shows that elements in
\Lambda_{st}
act freely by contraction and so WLOG we will
assume
\Lambda_{st}=\mathbbm{k}
(and thus
K_{t}=K(\rho_{t}t(\rho_{t})^{e},\rho_{s}^{e})(1)
) for the remainder of this paper to make notation easier.

To distinguish the terms
\rho_{s}^{e}
and
\rho_{t}t(\rho_{t})^{e}
in the differential for
\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{R^{e}}(K(\rho_{t}t(\rho_{t})^{e},\rho_{s}^{e})(1),\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))
as
\underline{w}
varies, let

\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w}):\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w})\to\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w})\quad\quad\rho_{t}t(\rho_{t})^{e}(\underline{w}):\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w})\to\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w})

Explicitly,
K(\rho_{t}t(\rho_{t})^{e},\rho_{s}^{e})(1)
is the complex

0\to\underline{\rho_{s}\wedge\rho_{t}t(\rho_{t})}(1)\boxtimes R^{e}\xrightarrow{\begin{bmatrix}-\rho_{t}t(\rho_{t})^{e}\\
\rho_{s}^{e}\end{bmatrix}}\underline{\rho_{s}}(1)\boxtimes R^{e}\oplus\underline{\rho_{t}t(\rho_{t})}(1)\boxtimes R^{e}\xrightarrow{\begin{bmatrix}\rho_{s}^{e}\ &\rho_{t}t(\rho_{t})^{e}\end{bmatrix}}\boxed{\underline{1}(1)\boxtimes R^{e}}\to 0

(18)

And thus it follows that
\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{R^{e}}(K(\rho_{t}t(\rho_{t})^{e},\rho_{s}^{e}),\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))
will be the total complex of the following double complex

(19)

where the boxed term is in cohomological degree 0 and on the LHS an element
b\underline{1}
for
b\in\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w})
corresponds to the map sending
\underline{1}\boxtimes 1\otimes 1\in K(\rho_{t}t(\rho_{t})^{e},\rho_{s}^{e})
to
b
(likewise with
b\underline{\rho_{s}}
, etc) and on the RHS we have just replaced this by the corresponding internal degree, etc. It’s clear that the corresponding spectral sequence of the double complex degenerates at the
E_{2}
page and so taking horizontal cohomology first the
E_{1}
page will look like

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H^{0}(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{R^{e}}(K(\rho_{s}^{e}),\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w})))(3)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H^{1}(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{R^{e}}(K(\rho_{s}^{e}),\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w})))(5)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\boxed{H^{0}(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{R^{e}}(K(\rho_{s}^{e}),\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w})))\,(-1)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H^{1}(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{R^{e}}(K(\rho_{s}^{e}),\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w})))(1)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\rho_{t}t(\rho_{t})^{e}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\rho_{t}t(\rho_{t})^{e}}

(20)

In fact, we will show in
Section

3.2.3
that both arrows in
Eq.

20
are 0. The bottom left corner of the
E_{2}
page will compute
\mathrm{Ext}^{0,\bullet}_{R^{e}}(B_{t},\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))
and the top right corner will compute
\mathrm{Ext}^{2,\bullet}_{R^{e}}(B_{t},\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))
. The diagonal will give us a filtration on
\mathrm{Ext}^{1,\bullet}_{R^{e}}(B_{t},\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))
. However, we will show that both groups are free right
R
modules, and thus the filtration splits and the
E_{2}
page will also compute
\mathrm{Ext}^{1,\bullet}_{R^{e}}(B_{t},\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))
as well. For the remainder of this section we will work in the case
W=W_{\infty}
and will show later that the results also hold in the finite case
W=W_{m_{st}}
.

3.2.1
Computation of
H^{0}(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{R^{e}}(K(\rho_{s}^{e}),\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w})))

Throughout we will fix the total ordering on
W_{\infty}

\mathrm{id}<s<t<ts<st<\ldots

which refines the Bruhat order. For this section we will make the additional assumption

Assumption 3
.

\left\{\alpha_{s},\alpha_{t}\right\}
is linearly independent,
\mathrm{char}\ \mathbbm{k}=0
and
\mathfrak{h}
is a symmetric realization, i.e.
a_{st}=a_{ts}
.

Following Section 3 in
[
Eli16
]
, set
[2]=q+q^{-1}=-a_{st}=-a_{ts}
and let
[m]=\tfrac{q^{m}-q^{-m}}{q-q^{-1}}
for
m\in\mathbb{Z}^{\geq 0}
. It was shown in
[
Eli16
]
that
[m]
is in fact a polynomial in
[2]
, and thus
[m]\in\mathbbm{k}
is well defined given
a_{st}
.

Our computations below will use the light leaves basis for
\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w})
as a free right
R-
module, more information can be found in Section 12.4 of
[
EMTW20
]
. Here is a brief summary. For any subexpression
\underline{f}\subset\underline{w}
(A subexpression for
\underline{w}=(w_{1},\ldots w_{m})
is a string
\underline{f}=(f_{1},\ldots,f_{m})
where
f_{i}\in\left\{0,1\right\}
), let
r(\underline{f})=\underline{w}^{\underline{f}}\in W_{\infty}
. Then there is a (flipped) light leaf map

\overline{\mathrm{LL}}_{\underline{w},\underline{f}}:\mathrm{BS}(r(\underline{f}))\to\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w})

One technically needs to choose a reduced expression for
r(\underline{f})\in W
to make sense of above. However this isn’t that big of an issue. For the affine case there is only one reduced expression for any
x\in W_{\infty}
so
r(\underline{f})
is a well defined expression. For the finite case any two reduced expressions are related by braid moves and the only effect on the light leaf map will be the addition of various
2m_{st}-
valent morphisms.

Now let
c_{bot}=c_{id}\otimes_{R}\ldots\otimes_{R}c_{id}\in\mathrm{BS}(r(\underline{f}))
6
6

6

We will often abuse notation and let
c_{bot}
denote the corresponding element
c_{id}\otimes_{R}\ldots
for any choice of
\underline{f}
.
. Then the light leaves basis for
\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w})
is the set

\left\{\mathrm{L}_{\underline{w},\underline{f}}=\overline{\mathrm{LL}}_{\underline{w},\underline{f}}(c_{bot})\ |\ \underline{f}\subset\underline{w}\right\}

Lemma 3.7
.

Arrange the light leaves basis based on
r(\underline{f})
from least to greatest in the total ordering on
W
indicated above (can choose an arbitrary order on those elements with the same
r(\underline{f})
). In this basis, the matrix for
\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w})
as a right
R
module will be upper triangular with diagonal entries equal to
r(\underline{e})^{-1}(\rho_{s})-\rho_{s}
.

Proof.

The proof of Proposition 12.26 in
[
EMTW20
]
shows

\rho_{s}\cdot\mathrm{L}_{\underline{w},\underline{e}}=\mathrm{L}_{\underline{w},\underline{e}}\cdot r(\underline{e})^{-1}(\rho_{s})+\sum_{\underline{w}^{\underline{f^{\prime}}}<r(\underline{e})}\mathrm{L}_{\underline{w},\underline{f^{\prime}}}a_{f^{\prime}}\quad\quad a_{f^{\prime}}\in R

(21)

and thus the lemma follows.
∎

Corollary 3.8
.

When
m_{st}=\infty
, the image of
\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w}):\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w})\to\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w})
is a free right
R
module and the kernel is also a free right
R
module with basis given by
\left\{\mathrm{L}_{\underline{w},\underline{f}}\,|r(\underline{f})=\mathrm{id}\textnormal{ or }t\right\}
.

Proof.

By
Lemma

3.7
we can find a right
R
basis for
\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w})
such that
\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w})
is upper triangular with diagonal entries equal to
r(\underline{e})^{-1}(\rho_{s})-\rho_{s}
. It is clear that when
r(\underline{e})=id\textnormal{ or }t
that this expression is 0; we claim in all other cases, this will not be zero. One can easily check by induction that

\displaystyle s(ts)^{m}(\rho_{s})

\displaystyle=\rho_{s}-\sum_{k=0}^{m}(st)^{k}(\alpha_{s})

(22)

\displaystyle(ts)^{m}(\rho_{s})

\displaystyle=\rho_{s}-\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}t(st)^{k}(\alpha_{s})

(23)

By Claim 3.5 in
[
Eli16
]
, one then computes that

\displaystyle s(ts)^{m}(\rho_{s})-\rho_{s}

\displaystyle=-\sum_{k=0}^{m}\left([2k+1]\alpha_{s}+[2k]\alpha_{t}\right)

(24)

\displaystyle(ts)^{m}(\rho_{s})-\rho_{s}

\displaystyle=-\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\left([2k+1]\alpha_{s}+[2k+2]\alpha_{t}\right)

(25)

To show
Eq.

24
and
Eq.

25
are nonzero, as
\alpha_{s},\alpha_{t}
are linearly independent, it suffices to show the sums

O_{m}=\sum_{k=0}^{m}[2k+1]\quad\quad E_{m}=\sum_{k=0}^{m}[2k]

don’t simultaneously vanish. Similarly, to show
Eq.

25
is nonzero it suffices to show
O_{m-1}
and
E_{m}
don’t simultaneously vanish. Depending on the realization there are two cases. First if
q=\pm 1
, it’s clear that
O_{m},E_{m}
is never zero for
m\geq 0,m\geq 1
respectively, in characteristic zero. Now for
q\neq\pm 1
, one computes that

\displaystyle O_{m}

\displaystyle=\frac{q+q^{3}+\ldots+q^{2m+1}-q^{-1}-q^{-3}-\ldots-q^{-(2m+1)}}{q-q^{-1}}

\displaystyle=\frac{1-q^{2m+2}+1-q^{-(2m+2)}}{(1-q^{-2})(1-q^{2})}=-\frac{(q^{m+1}-q^{-(m+1)})^{2}}{(1-q^{-2})(1-q^{2})}

\displaystyle E_{m}

\displaystyle=\frac{q^{2}+q^{4}+\ldots+q^{2m}-q^{-2}-q^{-4}-\ldots-q^{-(2m)}}{q-q^{-1}}=\frac{q^{2}-q^{-2m}+1-q^{2m+2}}{(q-q^{-1})(1-q^{2})}

\displaystyle=\frac{q^{-2m}(q^{2m+2}-1)-(q^{2m+2}-1)}{(q-q^{-1})(1-q^{2})}=\frac{(q^{-2m}-1)(q^{2m+2}-1)}{(q-q^{-1})(1-q^{2})}

It follows that
O_{m}=0\iff q^{2m+2}=1
and
E_{m}=0\iff q^{2m}=1\textnormal{ or }q^{2m+2}=1
. It follows that

\lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{stsrhos}=0\iff q^{2m+2}=1\quad\quad\lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{tsrhos}=0\iff q^{2m}=1

(26)

But, as noted in
[
Eli16
]
, a realization for
W_{\infty}
will be a realization for
W_{k}

\iff

q^{2k}=1
. Thus for
\mathfrak{h}
to be a (faithful )realization for
W_{\infty}

q^{2m}\neq 1\ \forall m\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}
and thus
Eq.

24
is never 0 for
m\geq 0
and
Eq.

25
is never zero for
m\geq 1
.

Now note that when
r(\underline{e})=id\textnormal{ or }t
not only does
r(\underline{e})^{-1}(\rho_{s})-\rho_{s}=0
, but in fact
\mathrm{L}_{\underline{w},\underline{e}}\in\ker\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w})
. This is clear from the diagrammatic picture as
r(\underline{e})
corresponds to the red or blue lines protruding below
\mathrm{L}_{\underline{w},\underline{e}}
and it is precisely these lines which we need to slide
\rho_{s}
from left to right over.

Therefore the image of
\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w})
will be the span of
\left\{\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w})(\mathrm{L}_{\underline{w},\underline{f}})\,|r(\underline{f})\neq id\textnormal{ or }t\right\}
. As shown above, we can arrange these vectors into a matrix that is upper triangular with nonzero entries on the diagonal.
Because
R
is a domain this will imply that
\left\{\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w})(\mathrm{L}_{\underline{w},\underline{f}})\,|r(\underline{f})\neq id\textnormal{ or }t\right\}
is linearly independent over
R
and therefore free. It then follows that
\ker\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w})
is generated by
\left\{\mathrm{L}_{\underline{w},\underline{f}}\,|r(\underline{f})=id\textnormal{ or }t\right\}
and thus is a basis.
∎

3.2.2
Computation of
H^{1}(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{R^{e}}(K(\rho_{s}^{e}),\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w})))

In this section we will use the 01-basis for
\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w})
as defined in Chapter 12 of
[
EMTW20
]
. In particular for
\underline{w}=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{m})
,
c_{bot}
as defined in
Section

3.2.1
and

c_{top}=c_{s_{1}}\otimes_{R}\ldots\otimes_{R}c_{s_{m}}\in\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w})

are two special elements in this basis.

Definition 3.9
.

Define
\mathrm{Tr}:\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w})\to R
by sending any element
b
to the coefficient of
c_{top}
when
b
is expressed in the 01-basis as a right
R-
module.

Definition 3.10
.

The global intersection form on
\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w})
is the
R-
valued pairing

\left\langle-,-\right\rangle:\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w})\times\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w})\to R

defined by

\left\langle a,b\right\rangle=\mathrm{Tr}(ab)

The global intersection form on
\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w})
is non-degenerate as seen in
[
EMTW20
, Section 18.2.2.2]
and gives an isomorphism
D_{\underline{w}}:\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w})\cong\mathbb{D}(\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))
sending
v\mapsto\left\langle v,-\right\rangle
.

Recall that in
Corollary

3.8
we found a right
R
basis for
\ker\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w})
given by
\left\{\mathrm{L}_{\underline{w},\underline{f}}\,|r(\underline{f})=\mathrm{id}\textnormal{ or }t\right\}
. For
\underline{f}=00\ldots
, we clearly have
r(\underline{f})=\mathrm{id}
and the corresponding light leaves will be all start dots, i.e. the element
c_{s_{1}}\otimes_{R}\ldots\otimes_{R}c_{s_{m}}
which is exactly
c_{top}
in the 01-basis. One can easily check that the dual basis vector under the global intersection form will be
c_{bot}
which we now denote

1(\underline{w}):=c_{id}\otimes_{R}\ldots\otimes_{R}c_{id}\in\mathbb{D}(\ker\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w}))

Definition 3.11
.

Let
\mathbb{D}:R^{e}-\mathrm{gmod}\to R^{e}-\mathrm{gmod}
be the functor

\mathbb{D}(N):=\mathrm{Hom}_{\_R}(N,R)

where
\_R
means we take right
R
module homomorphisms. This has a
R^{e}-\mathrm{gmod}
structure defined as
(r\cdot f\cdot r^{\prime})(b):=r\cdot f(b)\cdot r^{\prime}
.

Theorem 3.12
.

We have an isomorphism of right
R
modules

H^{1}(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{R^{e}}(K(\rho_{s}^{e}),\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w})))\cong\mathbb{D}(\ker\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w}))

Proof.

We have a commutative diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{D}(\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{D}(\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D_{\underline{w}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D_{\underline{w}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{D}(\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w}))}

(27)

which follows from adjointness of the global intersection form with multiplication by elements of
R
. As
D_{\underline{w}}
is an isomorphism it follows that

H^{1}(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{R^{e}}(K(\rho_{s}^{e}),\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w})))=\mathrm{coker\ }\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w})\cong\mathrm{coker\ }\mathbb{D}(\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w}))
. From
Corollary

3.8

\mathrm{im}\,\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w})
is a free right
R-
module and so we have a SES

0\to\mathbb{D}(\mathrm{im}\,\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w}))\xrightarrow{\mathbb{D}(\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w}))}\mathbb{D}(\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))\to\mathbb{D}(\ker\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w}))\to 0

and thus it follows that
\mathrm{coker\ }\mathbb{D}(\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w}))\cong\mathbb{D}(\ker\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w}))
.
∎

3.2.3
Computation of
H^{\bullet}(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{R^{e}}(K(\rho_{t}t(\rho_{t})^{e},\rho_{s}^{e}),\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w})))

Using

3.12
,
Eq.

20
which is the

page of the spectral sequence computing

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ker\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w})(3)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{D}(\ker\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w}))(5)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\boxed{\ker\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w})\,(-1)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{D}(\ker\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w}))(1)}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D_{\underline{w}}(\rho_{t}t(\rho_{t})^{e}(\underline{w}))|_{\ker\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w})}}

We claim that both vertical arrows above are 0. From

we know that

\left\{\mathrm{L}_{\underline{w},\underline{f}}=\overline{LL}_{\underline{w},\underline{f}}(c_{bot})\,|r(\underline{f})=id\textnormal{ or }t\right\}

It follows that

aka

as we can always slide

over to the other side.

For the right hand
\rho_{t}t(\rho_{t})^{e}
note that replacing

still produces a commutative diagram. It follows that for any

where the last equality follows from the previous paragraph. Thus from

3.6
we see that

Theorem 3.13
.

When
m_{st}=\infty
and
\Lambda_{st}=\mathbbm{k}
we have an isomorphism of right
R-

\displaystyle\mathrm{Ext}^{0,\bullet}_{R^{e}}(B_{t},\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))

\displaystyle\cong\ker\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w})\underline{1}(-1)\cong\ker\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w})(-1)

\displaystyle\mathrm{Ext}^{1,\bullet}_{R^{e}}(B_{t},\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))

\displaystyle\cong\ker\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w})\underline{\rho_{t}t(\rho_{t})}(-1)\oplus\widetilde{\mathbb{D}(\ker\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w}))}\underline{\rho_{s}}(-1)

\displaystyle\cong\ker\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w})(3)\oplus\widetilde{\mathbb{D}(\ker\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w}))}(1)

\displaystyle\mathrm{Ext}^{2,\bullet}_{R^{e}}(B_{t},\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))

\displaystyle\cong\mathbb{D}(\ker\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w}))\underline{\rho_{s}\wedge\rho_{t}t(\rho_{t})}(-1)\cong\mathbb{D}(\ker\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w}))(5)

Proof.

The fact that both arrows going up in

28
are 0 immediately gives the result for

and
\mathrm{Ext}^{2,\bullet}_{R^{e}}(B_{t},\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))
. For

, the spectral sequence gives the filtration

and since

is a free right

∎

Remark
.

The maps
\mathbb{D}(\ker\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w}))\underline{\rho_{s}}
are not chain maps and thus our notation
\widetilde{\mathbb{D}(\ker\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w}))}\underline{\rho_{s}}
means we need to choose a

s.t.
\rho_{t}t(\rho_{t})^{e}(w)=\rho_{s}^{e}(v)
for
w\in\mathbb{D}(\ker\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w}))
. However after we introduce
\Phi_{t}^{\underline{w}}
in

4.2
, we will have a preferred choice. Namely, if
\mathrm{LL}_{w}
is a light leaf morphism sending
c_{bot}\in\mathrm{BS}(\underline{v})
to
w
, then
\widetilde{w}\underline{\rho_{s}}
will be the morphism
\mathrm{LL}_{w}\circ\Phi_{t}^{\underline{v}}
.

4
New Generator and Relations:
m_{st}=\infty

We will continue to assume that
1
,
2
, and
3
hold in this section.

4.1
Affine Dimension 1 Calculations

Definition 4.1
.

An expression is called non repeating if there are no subexpressions of the form
ss\ldots
or
tt\ldots
.

Definition 4.2
.

Let
|\underline{w}|
be the number of elements in the expression
\underline{w}
.

Lemma 4.3
.

Suppose
m_{st}=\infty
and
\underline{w}
is a non repeating expression. If
|\underline{w}|
is odd, then the lowest internal degree element in
\mathrm{Hom}_{R^{e}}(R,\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))
is of degree 1. If
|\underline{w}|
is even, then the lowest internal degree element in
\mathrm{Hom}_{R^{e}}(R,\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))
is of degree 2.

Proof.

It suffices to show the case when
|\underline{w}|
is even as when
|\underline{w}|
is odd
\underline{w}=(t,\ldots,t)
or
(s,\ldots,s)
and we have the following natural isomorphism of graded vector spaces

\displaystyle\mathrm{Hom}_{R^{e}}(R,\mathrm{BS}(t,\ldots,t))

\displaystyle\cong\mathrm{Hom}_{R^{e}}(B_{t},\mathrm{BS}(t,\ldots))\cong\mathrm{Hom}_{R^{e}}(B_{t}\otimes_{R}B_{t},\mathrm{BS}(\ldots))

\displaystyle\cong\mathrm{Hom}_{R^{e}}(B_{t},\mathrm{BS}(t,\ldots)(1))\oplus\mathrm{Hom}_{R^{e}}(B_{t},\mathrm{BS}(t,\ldots)(-1))

and so the lowest internal degree element in
\mathrm{Hom}_{R^{e}}(R,\mathrm{BS}(t,\ldots,t))
is precisely 1 less than the lowest internal degree element in
\mathrm{Hom}_{R^{e}}(B_{t},\mathrm{BS}(t,\ldots))
,

We now proceed by induction on
|\underline{w}|
and use the diagrammatic description of
\mathrm{Hom}_{R^{e}}(R,\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))
. As
|\underline{w}|
is even the first and last element of
\underline{w}
are not the same and so the lowest internal degree element in
\mathrm{Hom}_{R^{e}}(R,\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))
must decompose as

\ \boxed{\phantom{a}a\phantom{a}}\ \ \boxed{\phantom{a}c\phantom{a}}

where
\ \boxed{\phantom{a}a\phantom{a}}\in\mathrm{Hom}_{R^{e}}(R,\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w^{\prime}}))
and
\ \boxed{\phantom{a}c\phantom{a}}\in\mathrm{Hom}_{R^{e}}(R,\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w^{\prime\prime}}))
such that
(\underline{w^{\prime}},\underline{w^{\prime\prime}})=\underline{w}
because morphisms are only generated by red and blue trivalent vertices and dots when
m_{st}=\infty
. First assume that both
|\underline{w^{\prime}}|
and
|\underline{w^{\prime\prime}}|
are odd. Notice that
\ \boxed{\phantom{a}a\phantom{a}}
has to be the lowest internal degree element in
\mathrm{Hom}_{R^{e}}(R,\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w^{\prime}}))
as otherwise we can replace it with the lowest. Same for
\ \boxed{\phantom{a}c\phantom{a}}
. Therefore by induction they both have degree 1 and thus the lowest degree element in
\mathrm{Hom}_{R^{e}}(R,\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))
has degree 2.

Now if
|\underline{w^{\prime}}|
and
|\underline{w^{\prime\prime}}|
are both even, one can show that it can’t be the lowest internal degree element as there will exist dots (because
m_{st}=\infty
) which can be turned into trivalent vertices, which lowers the degree.
∎

Lemma 4.4
.

For
m_{st}=\infty
let
\underline{w}
be any expression and let
m(t,\underline{w})
be any non repeating subexpression of
t\underline{w}
such that
|m(t,\underline{w})|
is maximal among all non repeating subexpressions of
t\underline{w}
. If
|m(t,\underline{w})|
is odd, then the lowest internal degree element of
\ker\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w})(-1)
is
-|\underline{w}|+|m(t,\underline{w})|
. If
|m(t,\underline{w})|
is even, then the lowest internal degree element of
\ker\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w})(-1)
is
1-|\underline{w}|+|m(t,\underline{w})|
.

Proof.

As
\ker\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w})(-1)\cong\mathrm{Hom}_{R^{e}}(B_{t},\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))
it suffices to show the lowest degree in
\mathrm{Hom}_{R^{e}}(B_{t},\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))
is as prescribed above. Note

\mathrm{Hom}_{R^{e}}(B_{t},\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))\cong\mathrm{Hom}_{R^{e}}(R,B_{t}\otimes_{R}\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))

Choose some
m(t,\underline{w})
as defined above. Then the part of
t\underline{w}
excluding
m(t,\underline{w})
has to be of the form
ss\ldots
or
tt\ldots
. As
B_{s}\otimes_{R}B_{s}\cong B_{s}(1)\oplus B_{s}(-1)
, we can then simplify
B_{t}\otimes_{R}\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w})
to
\mathrm{BS}(m(t,\underline{w}))
at the cost of some grading shifts. As there are exactly
|t\underline{w}|-|m(t,\underline{w})|=1+|\underline{w}|-|m(t,\underline{w})|
places in
t\underline{w}
where we need to apply this relation, it follows that

\underline{\mathrm{rk}}\ \ \mathrm{Hom}_{R^{e}}(B_{t},\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))=\underline{\mathrm{rk}}\ \ (v+v^{-1})^{1+|\underline{w}|-|m(t,\underline{w})|}\mathrm{Hom}_{R^{e}}(R,\mathrm{BS}(m(t,\underline{w})))

Now apply the previous lemma.
∎

Proposition 4.5
.

For
m_{st}=\infty
,
\mathrm{Ext}^{1,-(|\underline{w}|+1)}_{R^{e}}(B_{t},\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))
is a 1 dimensional
\mathbbm{k}
module when
|m(t,\underline{w})|\geq 4
.

Proof.

Under the decomposition from
Theorem

3.13

\mathrm{Ext}^{1,-(|\underline{w}|+1)}_{R^{e}}(B_{t},\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w})))\cong\ker\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w})(3)_{-|\underline{w}|-1}\oplus\widetilde{\mathbb{D}(\ker\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w}))}(1)_{-|\underline{w}|-1}

\mathbb{D}(\ker\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w}))(1)_{-|\underline{w}|-1}
is a
1
dimensional
\mathbbm{k}
module, as
1(\underline{w})
is the lowest degree element in
\mathbb{D}(\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))\cong\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w})
and we showed above that
1(\underline{w})\in\mathbb{D}(\ker\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w}))
. Thus it suffices to show the lowest degree element in
\ker\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w})(3)
is greater than this. By
Lemma

4.4
, we see that when
|m(t,\underline{w})|
is odd, the lowest degree element in
\ker\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w})(3)
will be
-|\underline{w}|+|m(t,\underline{w})|-4
and thus we want

-|\underline{w}|+|m(t,\underline{w})|-4>-|\underline{w}|-1\implies|m(t,\underline{w})|>3

Similarily we find that when
|m(t,\underline{w})|
is even, we want

-|\underline{w}|+|m(t,\underline{w})|-3>-|\underline{w}|-1\implies|m(t,\underline{w})|>2

and thus
|m(t,\underline{w})|\geq 4
encompasses both cases above.
∎

4.2
The New Generator

Lemma 4.6
.

Suppose we have a double complex
C^{\bullet,\bullet}
with differentials and terms pictured below
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\boxed{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g^{\prime}}

(where
C^{0,0}=X
is boxed) such that

(1)

\ker f\subset\ker g

(2)

\mathrm{im}\,g^{\prime}\subset\mathrm{im}\,f^{\prime}

(3)

\ker f^{\prime}=0

Then
H^{1}(\mathrm{Tot}(C^{\bullet,\bullet}))\cong Y/\mathrm{im}\,f
. Precisely this means that

•

Any
y\in Y
extends to a unique 1-cocycle
(y,z)\in Y\times Z
in
\mathrm{Tot}(C^{\bullet,\bullet})

•

two 1-cocycles
(y,z)
and
(y^{\prime},z^{\prime})
define the same class in
H^{1}(\mathrm{Tot}(C^{\bullet,\bullet}))\iff y\equiv y^{\prime}
in
Y/im(f)

Proof.

Straightforward from assumptions.
∎

Remark
.

Even without the assumptions
(1)-(3)
above, if
y\in\mathrm{im}\,(f)
and
(y,z)
is any cocycle, then
(y,z)\equiv(0,0)
in
H^{1}(\mathrm{Tot}(C^{\bullet,\bullet}))
and similarly if
z\in\mathrm{im}\,(g)
and
(y,z)
is any cocycle, then
(y,z)\equiv(0,0)
in
H^{1}(\mathrm{Tot}(C^{\bullet,\bullet}))
. This follows from the definition of
(y,z)
being a cocycle.

Remark
.

To prevent notation overload, some of the relations in the following subsections are “incorrectly written”. Specifically, on one side of a relation will end up in
\mathrm{KS}(\underline{w})
for some
\underline{w}=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{m})
and the other side will end up in
\mathrm{KS}(\underline{w})\otimes_{R}K_{\varnothing}
or
K_{\varnothing}\otimes_{R}\mathrm{KS}(\underline{w})
, etc. This happens when the relation involves the counit
\widetilde{\epsilon_{s}}:K_{s}\to K_{\varnothing}
for instance. One then needs to apply a chain lift of the right unitor
\widetilde{\theta_{s}}
or the left unitor
\widetilde{\lambda_{s}}
to one side to have actual equality. We will do this in the calculations by replacing
\mathrm{id}_{\underline{w}}\otimes_{R}\widetilde{\epsilon_{s}}
with

\mathrm{id}_{\underline{w}}\otimes_{R}\widetilde{\epsilon_{s}^{\prime}}:=(\mathrm{id}_{(s_{1},\ldots,s_{m_{1}})}\otimes_{R}\widetilde{\theta_{s_{m}}})\circ(\mathrm{id}_{\underline{w}}\otimes_{R}\widetilde{\epsilon_{s}}):\mathrm{KS}(\underline{w})\otimes_{R}K_{s}\to\mathrm{KS}(\underline{w})\otimes_{R}K_{\varnothing}\to\mathrm{KS}(\underline{w})

in the case of
\mathrm{KS}(\underline{w})\otimes_{R}K_{\varnothing}
in our calculations. In fact, we will always end up in the cohomological degree 0 part of
\mathrm{KS}(\underline{w})\otimes_{R}K_{\varnothing}
after applying
\mathrm{id}_{\underline{w}}\otimes_{R}\widetilde{\epsilon_{s}}
and so explicitly we then apply

(\mathrm{id}_{(s_{1},\ldots,s_{m_{1}})}\otimes_{R}\widetilde{\theta_{s_{m}}}^{0})(\underline{1}\boxtimes a_{1}\otimes\ldots\otimes a_{m+1}\otimes a_{m+2})=\underline{1}\boxtimes a_{1}\otimes\ldots\otimes a_{m+1}a_{m+2}

and similarily with
K_{\varnothing}\otimes_{R}\mathrm{KS}(\underline{w})
, etc.

For more background on cyclicity we refer the reader to

, Chapter 7.5]

. The main upshot of having a cyclic morphism is the following theorem

Theorem 4.22

[
CKS00
]
)
.

Given a string diagram

representing a cyclic 2-morphism between 1-morphisms with chosen biadjoints, any isotopy of
D
fixing endpoints represents the same 2-morphism.

We should be careful in applying this theorem however. Let
\partial
denote the diagram on the RHS below and note that

is isotopic “fixing endpoints” to

and these do turn out to be equal in

. However, this is not a consequence of cyclicity! The diagram on the RHS is technically not a string diagram, so
Theorem

4.22
doesn’t apply. A string diagram representing the RHS is drawn below

s
\partial
ss

and now it is clear that the LHS of
Eq.

31
isn’t an isotopy of the above string diagram. In general if adding a cap on top and a cup on bottom “doesn’t change” the morphism, we will say it is rotation invariant. For example,
Eq.

31
are equal due to rotation invariance. Rotation invariance of a morphism greatly simplifies the graphical calculus for a morphism because it implies we don’t need to do this bookkeeping above on how the morphism was constructed, we only need to care about the color(s) of the morphism (See the proof of

).

Theorem 5.1
.

Assume all quantum numbers are invertible. Then there is an isomorphism of right
R
modules.

\displaystyle\mathrm{Ext}^{0,\bullet}_{R^{e}}(R,B_{{}_{t}\widehat{k}})

\displaystyle\cong R(-k)

\displaystyle\mathrm{Ext}^{1,\bullet}_{R^{e}}(R,B_{{}_{t}\widehat{k}})

\displaystyle\cong R(4-k)\oplus R(k)

\displaystyle\mathrm{Ext}^{2,\bullet}_{R^{e}}(R,B_{{}_{t}\widehat{k}})

\displaystyle\cong R(k+4)

Proof.

Proceed by induction on
k
.
k=1
follows from
Theorem

3.13
. From
Theorem

3.13
we know that

\displaystyle\mathrm{Ext}^{0,\bullet}_{R^{e}}(R,\mathrm{BS}({}_{t}\widehat{\underline{k}}))

\displaystyle\cong\ker\rho_{s}^{e}({}_{s}\widehat{\underline{k-1}})(-1)

\displaystyle\mathrm{Ext}^{1,\bullet}_{R^{e}}(R,\mathrm{BS}({}_{t}\widehat{\underline{k}}))

\displaystyle\cong\ker\rho_{s}^{e}({}_{s}\widehat{\underline{k-1}})(-1)(4)\oplus\mathbb{D}(\ker\rho_{s}^{e}({}_{s}\widehat{\underline{k-1}})(-1))

(45)

\displaystyle\mathrm{Ext}^{2,\bullet}_{R^{e}}(R,\mathrm{BS}({}_{t}\widehat{\underline{k}}))

\displaystyle\cong\mathbb{D}(\ker\rho_{s}^{e}({}_{s}\widehat{\underline{k-1}})(-1))(4)

(46)

In other words,
\mathrm{Ext}^{\bullet,\bullet}_{R^{e}}(R,\mathrm{BS}({}_{t}\widehat{\underline{k}}))
satisfies the pattern as prescribed by the theorem. Because all quantum numbers are invertible, we have a decomposition

\mathrm{BS}({}_{t}\widehat{\underline{k}})\cong B_{{}_{t}\widehat{k}}\bigoplus_{y<{}_{t}\widehat{k}}B_{y}^{\oplus h_{y}}

(47)

By Soergel’s Hom formula we know that
\mathrm{Ext}^{0,\bullet}_{R^{e}}(R,B_{{}_{t}\widehat{k}})\cong R(-k)
. Therefore

\ker\rho_{s}^{e}({}_{s}\widehat{\underline{k-1}})(-1)=\mathrm{Ext}^{0,\bullet}_{R^{e}}(R,\mathrm{BS}({}_{t}\widehat{\underline{k}}))\cong R(-k)\bigoplus\mathrm{Ext}^{0,\bullet}_{R^{e}}(R,B_{y}^{\oplus h_{y}})

By induction
\mathrm{Ext}^{\bullet,\bullet}_{R^{e}}(R,B_{y}^{\oplus h_{y}})
will also satisfy the pattern as prescribed by the theorem and so subtracting
\mathrm{Ext}^{\bullet,\bullet}_{R^{e}}(R,B_{y}^{\oplus h_{y}})
from both sides of
Eq.

45
and
Eq.

46
we complete the induction.
∎

Recall from
Theorem

3.13
that we have the isomorphism

\mathrm{Ext}^{1,\bullet}_{R^{e}}(B_{t},\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))\cong\ker\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w})\underline{\rho_{t}t(\rho_{t})}(-1)\oplus\widetilde{\mathbb{D}(\ker\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w}))}\underline{\rho_{s}}(-1)

where

means the morphism consists of

only identity morphisms
(aka straight lines). This is because in the light leaf algorithm,
in the affine case
, we generate generalized pitchforks whenever a decoration is of the form
D0
or
D1
. As a result, we only need to consider the light leaves that are made up of only dots (

). However, suppose that at step
i
of our stroll, the corresponding decorations ends in
U1U0
. It will follow the decoration at the next step has to be either
D0
or
D1
but this isn’t allowed, or
i=k-2
and we end the algorithm at the next step. In other words, we must have all lines after the appearance of the first line or all lines with a dot at the end, which is exactly what is depicted in
Eq.

51
.

(57)

Rotation invariance will imply that the red
2k-
extvalent morphism is cyclic. Hochschild dots were shown to be cyclic in
[
Mak22
]
Section 4, and the other generating morphisms are also cyclic so by Proposition 7.18 in
[
EMTW20
]
an isotopy class of diagrams in
\mathscr{D}^{\mathrm{Ext}}_{\infty}
unambiguously represents a morphism in
\mathscr{D}^{\mathrm{Ext}}_{\infty}
. As a result, any diagram isotopic or rotationally equivalent to the remaining relations will also hold in
\mathscr{D}^{\mathrm{Ext}}_{\infty}
.

Lemma 7.1
.

When

.

\displaystyle\mathrm{Ext}^{0,\bullet}_{R^{e}}(B_{t},\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))

\displaystyle\mathrm{Ext}^{1,\bullet}_{R^{e}}(B_{t},\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))

Remark
.

The statements above for the finite case mirror the affine case word for word, but there’s a subtle difference. Namely in the finite case, for a given expression
\underline{w}
and subexpression
\underline{f}
, the light leaf morphism
\mathrm{L}_{\underline{w},\underline{f}}
is possibly different than the affine case. For example, consider
\underline{w}=(s,t,s,t,s)
and
\underline{f}=(1,1,1,1,1)
. When
m_{st}=\infty
The light leaf algorithm then returns the diagram on the left below

while for
m_{st}=3
the light leaf algorithm returns the diagram on the right above. In particular
r((1,1,1,1,1))=t
and so by
Lemma

7.1
for
m_{st}=3
,
\mathrm{L}_{(s,t,s,t,s),(1,1,1,1,1)}\in\ker\rho_{s}^{e}((s,t,s,t,s))
and so by
Theorem

7.2
corresponds to a morphism in
\mathrm{Ext}^{0,\bullet}_{R^{e}}(B_{t},\mathrm{BS}(s,t,s,t,s))
. Of course this is nothing more the
6-
valent morphism, but where 2 of the strands have been twisted up.

To summarize, in the finite case
\ker\rho_{s}^{e}(\underline{w})
is possibly larger and consequently the groups
\mathrm{Ext}^{\bullet,\bullet}_{R^{e}}(B_{t},\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))
are also possibly larger.

7.1
Dimension 1 Calculations

Lemma 7.3
.

Suppose
m_{st}<\infty
and suppose
\underline{w}
is a non repeating expression. If
|\underline{w}|<2m_{st}
, then the lowest internal degree element in
\mathrm{Hom}_{R^{e}}(R,\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))
is of degree 1, 2 if
|\underline{w}|
is odd, even respectively. If
|\underline{w}|\geq 2m_{st}
the lowest internal degree element in
\mathrm{Hom}_{R^{e}}(R,\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))
is of degree
2m_{st}-|\underline{w}|
.

Proof.

For
|\underline{w}|<2m_{st}
,
\underline{\mathrm{rk}}\ \ \mathrm{Hom}_{R^{e}}(R,\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))
agrees with the affine case (one can use Soergel’s Hom formula and then use Lemma 3.19 in
[
EMTW20
]
and biadjointness of
b_{s}
with the standard form so that one never needs to use the braid relation in the finite Hecke algebra) so this follows from
Lemma

4.3
. Now, let
\mathrm{LD}(\mathrm{BS}(\underline{v}),\mathrm{BS}(\underline{u}))
be the lowest degree morphism in
\mathrm{Hom}_{R^{e}}(\mathrm{BS}(\underline{v}),\mathrm{BS}(\underline{u}))
. Given any morphism
\mathrm{Hom}_{R^{e}}(B_{s},\mathrm{BS}(\underline{u}))
we can produce a morphism in
\mathrm{Hom}_{R^{e}}(R,\mathrm{BS}(\underline{u}))
by adding a dot to the bottom of
B_{s}
. As a result, we see that

\mathrm{LD}(R,B_{s}\otimes_{R}\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))=\mathrm{LD}(B_{s},\mathrm{BS}(\underline{u}))\geq\mathrm{LD}(R,\mathrm{BS}(\underline{u}))-1

Therefore each time we tensor with
B_{s}
or
B_{t}
the lowest degree drops by at most 1. It follows that when
|\underline{w}|\geq 2m_{st}
, the lowest degree element in
\mathrm{Hom}_{R^{e}}(R,\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))
is at least degree
2m_{st}-|\underline{w}|
. One can actually show it’s also at most
2m_{st}-|\underline{w}|
by explicity producing a morphism in
\mathrm{Hom}_{R^{e}}(R,\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}))
of this degree which we leave to the reader. For a hint, look at the RHS of
Eq.

73
.
∎

Proposition 7.4
.

For

,

We then have that an analogue of

4.4
holds by noting that the proof of
Lemma

4.4
still applies for

except we need to replace

with

in the last step. As a result, when

which is true when

as desired.
∎

.

\displaystyle\ldots

\underline{v}

\underline{v}
